42899937.text: Background Gravity redistributes pulmonary blood flow in the upright position; however, how total pulmonary vascular volume (TPVV) and its arterial and venous components depend on position remains unclear. Purpose To quantify position-dependent changes in TPVV and the corresponding arterial and venous components across lung lobes and vertical lung regions using upright chest CT. Materials and Methods This secondary analysis of a prospective, single-center study enrolled healthy adult volunteers who underwent same-day noncontrast chest CT in supine and upright positions using a 320-detector row CT system between March 2018 and December 2018. Participants were excluded for incidental lung abnormalities or inadequate vessel separation. Pulmonary arteries and veins were segmented semiautomatically, and pulmonary vascular volumes were quantified for whole lung, lobes, and upper, middle, and lower lung regions. Paired two-sided t tests with Bonferroni correction were used for comparisons. Results Fifty participants (mean age ± SD, 47 years ± 9.7; 28 men) were evaluated. Standing reduced TPVV by 18.8% compared with the supine position (mean, 99.8 mL ± 18.2 vs 81.0 mL ± 14.3; P < .001). When standing, pulmonary venous volume decreased more than pulmonary arterial volume across the whole lung (25.4% reduction [mean, 50.7 mL ± 9.1 supine vs 37.5 mL ± 5.7 standing] vs 11.1% reduction [mean, 49.1 mL ± 9.9 supine vs 43.6 mL ± 9.4 standing]; P < .001). Volume reductions when standing followed a craniocaudal gradient, with greater reductions in the upper lung than in the lower lung (P < .001). Dependent lower lung regions also showed decreases in TPVV (mean reduction, -12.0%; mean, 40.4 mL ± 9.0 supine vs 35.4 mL ± 7.7 standing), pulmonary arterial volume (mean reduction, -6.0%; mean, 18.2 mL ± 3.9 supine vs 17.1 mL ± 4.5 standing), and pulmonary venous volume (mean reduction, -16.7%; mean, 22.2 mL ± 4.6 supine vs 18.3 mL ± 3.7 standing; all P < .001). Conclusion Upright chest CT showed that, compared with the supine position, standing reduced TPVV, predominantly venous, with a vertical gradient, where dependent lower lung regions exhibited modest volume reduction.

42937537.text: Background Attenuation coefficient (AC) is an established US marker for assessing patients with liver steatosis. However, improvements in diagnostic performance are warranted. Purpose To evaluate the diagnostic performance of AC, normalized local variance (NLV), hepatorenal ratio, and their combinations for liver histopathologic steatosis in participants with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Materials and Methods This secondary analysis of the prospective Innovative Liver Elasticity, Attenuation, and Dispersion Ultrasound Study (iLEAD) (June 2019 to March 2023) included participants with biopsy-proven MASLD who underwent multiparametric liver US; AC, NLV, and hepatorenal ratio were measured. The diagnostic performance of each imaging marker and their combinations for determining steatosis grade were assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with the DeLong test, and reclassification improvement was also assessed using the category-free net reclassification improvement (NRI). Results A total of 102 participants (mean age, 52 years ± 16.1 [SD]; 51 male) were evaluated. AC showed the highest diagnostic performance for determining steatosis grade across all grades (AUC for grade ≥S1, 0.93 [95% CI: 0.87, 0.99]), compared with NLV (0.88 [95% CI: 0.77, 0.99]; P = .47) and hepatorenal ratio (0.85 [95% CI: 0.71, 0.98]; P = .30). Four models were constructed for identifying steatosis grades: model 1, AC only; model 2, AC plus NLV; model 3, AC plus hepatorenal ratio; model 4, AC plus NLV plus hepatorenal ratio. Models 2-4 showed no evidence of a difference in performance from model 1 for identifying grade S1 or higher (AUC, 0.93-0.98; P = .16, .15, and .07, respectively), but an improvement in risk reclassification was observed for model 4 (NRI, 1.18 [95% CI: 0.54, 1.77]; P < .001) compared with model 1 (reference). Performance was similar across models in identifying steatosis grade S2 or greater (AUC, 0.89-0.90; all P ≥ .47) and for grade S3 (AUC, 0.89-0.90; all P ≥ .72), but an improvement in risk reclassification was observed for model 3 compared with model 1 (≥S2 steatosis: NRI, 0.58 [95% CI: 0.20, 0.94] [P = .002]; S3 steatosis: NRI, 0.71 [95% CI: 0.26, 1.14] [P = .002]). Conclusion Liver US-derived AC performed better than NLV and hepatorenal ratio in determining steatosis grade in participants with MASLD; when these markers were combined, reclassification of steatosis grade improved.

42950937.label: Objective
42950937.text: Workup of low back pain (LBP) in emergency departments (EDs) commonly involves CT or MRI, even though guidelines reserve advanced imaging for patients with red flags. We measured how often urgent care center (UCC) radiography for low-acuity LBP was followed by advanced imaging in the ED within 30 days, and compared per-study resource intensity between UCC radiography and ED CT or MRI.

42950937.label: Methods
42950937.text: This retrospective cohort study included adults imaged for LBP at 23 UCCs and affiliated EDs between 2019 and 2025. We excluded red-flag presentations by screening keywords from the order indication. We identified 30-day returns by linking medical record numbers between cohorts, and two radiologists reviewed each one. Resource intensity was measured as Total Relative Value Units (RVU) per study, converted to approximate Medicare-allowed dollars.

42950937.label: Results
42950937.text: Among 16,754 studies (2,924 UCC radiographs, 13,830 ED studies) from 15,759 patients, UCC patients were younger (median 50 vs 67 years, P < 0.001). Median Total RVU was 1.43 (UCC) versus 5.14 (ED) (about $48 vs $171, P < 0.001). Twenty-four UCC studies were followed by ED advanced imaging within 30 days (0.82%, 95% CI 0.55-1.22), 12 within 24 hours. Radiologists judged one return a true radiographic miss. Return rates were similar across UCC networks (P = 1.00).

42950937.label: Discussion
42950937.text: UCC radiography for low-acuity LBP was rarely followed by ED advanced imaging within 30 days and entailed lower per-study imaging resource use than ED CT or MRI.

42955037.text: Biliary tract cancers, comprising gallbladder cancer and intrahepatic and extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, are uncommon but aggressive malignancies that are often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Accurate staging is critical because patients with localized disease may be candidates for curative resection, whereas those with unresectable or metastatic disease are triaged to systemic and palliative therapy. This document reviews the evidence for imaging in five clinical scenarios: locoregional staging of gallbladder cancer, locoregional staging of cholangiocarcinoma, staging of distant metastatic disease, posttreatment evaluation, and surveillance. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the abdomen are the mainstays of locoregional assessment, whereas CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and FDG-PET are used for distant staging and follow-up. The American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria are evidence-based guidelines for specific clinical conditions that are reviewed annually by a multidisciplinary expert panel. The guideline development and revision process support the systematic analysis of the medical literature from peer reviewed journals. Established methodology principles such as Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation or GRADE are adapted to evaluate the evidence. The RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method User Manual provides the methodology to determine the appropriateness of imaging and treatment procedures for specific clinical scenarios. In those instances where peer reviewed literature is lacking or equivocal, experts may be the primary evidentiary source available to formulate a recommendation.

42955837.text: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic fibroinflammatory cholangiopathy characterized by multifocal biliary strictures, cholestasis, and an increased risk of hepatobiliary malignancy and liver failure. MRI and MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) are central to diagnosis, surveillance, and risk stratification. Recent consensus guidelines from the International PSC Study Group emphasize standardized reporting for PSC with MRI and MRCP. Beyond anatomic assessment, established and emerging quantitative and functional imaging biomarkers include liver stiffness measurements, T1 mapping, extracellular volume fraction, and relative hepatobiliary phase enhancement. Imaging-based scoring systems such as Assessment of Noncontrast MRI for Advanced Liver Imaging (ANALI) scores provide additional prognostic information and correlate with clinical outcomes and established risk models. Hepatocyte-specific contrast-enhanced MRI allows evaluation of biliary excretion and regional liver function, facilitating identification of functional strictures and parenchymal dysfunction. The authors review current MRI and MRCP reporting standards, prognostic scoring systems, and evolving functional MRI techniques, with an emphasis on practical implementation in clinical radiology practice.

43034937.text: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is highly prevalent and frequently first recognized at ultrasound, but conventional B-mode assessment is limited by subjectivity and reduced sensitivity for mild steatosis. Quantitative ultrasound (QUS) techniques address these limitations by converting acoustic signal properties into numerical biomarkers of hepatic fat, including attenuation coefficient, backscatter coefficient, speed of sound, and composite measures. This review summarizes the technical principles, current evidence, clinical implementation, and limitations of ultrasound-based liver fat quantification techniques in MASLD. Their major advantages are accessibility, integration into routine ultrasound examinations, and potential use alongside elastography for multiparametric assessment. However, thresholds vary across vendors, software implementations, acquisition protocols, reference standards, and patient populations, limiting interchangeability and universal cutoffs. In clinical practice, ultrasound fat quantification should not be interpreted in isolation but integrated with fibrosis risk stratification and metabolic risk assessment. Further multicenter studies are needed to standardize acquisition and reporting, define clinically meaningful longitudinal changes, and link ultrasound-derived fat reduction with patient outcomes. QUS is therefore best regarded as an evolving, practical framework for objective steatosis assessment that complements, rather than replaces, comprehensive MASLD risk stratification. KEY POINTS: Question Conventional B-mode ultrasound is subjective and insensitive to mild hepatic steatosis, creating an unmet need for objective, reproducible liver fat quantification in MASLD. Findings Attenuation-based and composite quantitative ultrasound methods provide objective liver fat assessment, but vendor-dependent thresholds currently limit interchangeability and universal clinical application. Clinical relevance Quantitative ultrasound enables accessible, objective liver fat assessment during routine imaging, improving detection and grading of hepatic steatosis and supporting risk-based MASLD care; however, vendor-specific thresholds and acquisition variability require technique-specific interpretation.

43043187.text: Background Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema (CPFE) has heterogeneous outcomes, and visual assessment or separate measurement of emphysema and fibrosis does not directly identify which structural component predominates in an individual patient. Purpose To determine whether quantitative CT enables objective stratification of CPFE into fibrosis-dominant and emphysema-dominant phenotypes and to evaluate their distinct clinical trajectories and prognostic implications. Materials and Methods This secondary analysis of a prospective multicenter observational study included patients with CPFE enrolled between January 2017 and December 2024. A fixed commercial artificial intelligence workstation automatically segmented the lungs and quantified emphysema and fibrosis on high-resolution CT scans. Participants were classified as having the fibrosis-dominant phenotype when the fibrosis percentage was equal to or greater than the emphysema percentage, and as having the emphysema-dominant phenotype otherwise. Group comparisons used the t test, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, χ2 test, or Fisher exact test. Cox models were used to assess all-cause mortality; C index and calibration were used to assess model performance. Results The study population included 1583 participants (median age, 65 years [IQR, 58-71 years]; 1186 men); 823 (52%) had the fibrosis-dominant phenotype, and 760 (48%) had the emphysema-dominant phenotype. The fibrosis-dominant group had a higher fibrosis percentage than the emphysema-dominant group (median, 18% vs 10%; P < .001), whereas the emphysema-dominant group had a higher emphysema percentage (median, 7% vs 6%; P < .001). During a median follow-up of 2.59 years, 513 deaths occurred. The fibrosis-dominant phenotype was associated with higher mortality after adjustment (hazard ratio, 1.36 [95% CI: 1.13, 1.62]; P < .001). Conclusion Quantitative CT helped identify emphysema- and fibrosis-dominant CPFE phenotypes with different prognoses. The fibrosis-dominant phenotype was associated with higher all-cause mortality.

43043987.label: Background
43043987.text: High-risk plaque (HRP) features on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) predict future coronary events, yet the microstructural substrate underlying these radiological signatures remains largely unknown. Polarization-sensitive (PS) optical frequency domain imaging (OFDI) quantifies tissue birefringence and depolarization-derived lipid core burden index (LCBI) in vivo. We aimed to investigate the relationship between PS-OFDI-derived polarimetric signals and CCTA-defined HRP features.

43043987.label: Methods
43043987.text: We retrospectively identified 43 patients from a prospective registry of intracoronary polarimetry with PS-OFDI who had undergone CCTA before hospitalization and subsequently underwent OFDI-guided percutaneous coronary intervention. A total of 70 coronary segments were analyzed. HRP was defined as the presence of ≥2 established CCTA features: positive remodeling, low-attenuation plaque, napkin-ring sign, or spotty calcification. Conventional OFDI metrics and PS-OFDI-derived birefringence and depolarization-derived maximum 4-mm LCBI were evaluated in relation to CCTA-defined HRP. Segment-level comparisons accounted for within-patient clustering, and correlation and discrimination analyses incorporated patient-level bootstrap resampling.

43043987.label: Results
43043987.text: Among the 70 analyzed segments, 28 (40%) exhibited CCTA-defined HRP. HRP segments showed lower birefringence and higher depolarization-derived maximum 4-mm LCBI than non-HRP segments (both P<0.001). Birefringence was inversely correlated with low-attenuation plaque volume (ρ=-0.350 [95% CI, -0.543 to -0.131]), whereas depolarization-derived maximum 4-mm LCBI correlated with maximum lipid arc (ρ=0.480 [95% CI, 0.277-0.635]), lipid length (ρ=0.463 [95% CI, 0.199-0.654]), and minimum fibrous cap thickness (ρ=-0.466 [95% CI, -0.661 to -0.212]). Adding birefringence to conventional OFDI maximum lipid arc provided exploratory evidence of incremental discrimination for CCTA-defined HRP: apparent area under the curve increased from 0.673 to 0.853 (Δ area under the curve, 0.180 [95% CI, 0.049-0.370]), with the corresponding optimism-corrected area under the curves of 0.672 and 0.840.

43043987.label: Conclusions
43043987.text: PS-OFDI-derived metrics were associated with CCTA-defined HRP features and conventional OFDI lipid parameters. Reduced birefringence in HRP lesions suggests altered collagen organization as a potential microstructural substrate underlying adverse plaque morphology identified by CCTA.
